title: 'The Boat's Sunk': Kansas City Immigration Court Buried Under 40,000 Cases
excerpt: Attorneys in Kansas City warn that the only immigration court serving Missouri and Kansas is overwhelmed by a backlog KMBC puts at about 40,000 cases — with too few judges and too few lawyers for the people waiting on hearings.
body:
• Kansas City immigration attorneys are warning that the city's immigration court — the only one serving Missouri and Kansas — is overwhelmed by a backlog KMBC puts at about 40,000 cases, with staffing shortages compounding the delays.
  • The court's judges decide removal and asylum cases for two states. Earlier reporting counted three permanent judges at the court; the Justice Department's current court page lists five immigration judges.
  • There is no right to a government-appointed attorney in immigration court, and only 23.4% of immigrants nationally had a lawyer when ordered removed in May 2025, according to Transactional Records Access Clearinghouse data reported by The Pitch.
  • If you have a case at this court: confirm your hearing date before you travel — through EOIR's case information line at 800-898-7180 or the court's page at the Department of Justice — and keep your address updated with the court, because notices are mailed to the address on file.

Kansas City's immigration attorneys describe a court system overwhelmed by a backlog of roughly 40,000 cases, staffing shortages and deportation concerns, KMBC reported in a segment it titled "The boat's sunk." The Kansas City Immigration Court, housed on Grand Boulevard in downtown Kansas City, is the only immigration court in Missouri and Kansas, according to reporting by The Pitch — which means every removal and asylum case arising in two states funnels through a single courtroom suite.

Who is affected, and how the court works

Immigration courts are not part of the independent federal judiciary. The Kansas City court falls under the Executive Office for Immigration Review (EOIR) in the Department of Justice, and its judges decide whether the government can legally remove a person from the United States. The Justice Department's court page lists the court at 2345 Grand Boulevard, Suite 525, Kansas City, MO 64108, with public hours of 8 a.m. to 4 p.m., and currently names five immigration judges. KCTV's earlier reporting on the same court counted three permanent judges working through the backlog, with a military lawyer added as a temporary judge — a staffing picture local attorneys say has not kept pace with the caseload. Counts of the backlog itself have moved over time: The Pitch, citing Transactional Records Access Clearinghouse (TRAC) figures, put the court's pending cases at 52,533 in its 2025 reporting, within a national backlog of 3.5 million cases. KMBC's current reporting puts the figure attorneys are working against at about 40,000.

https://x.com/kmbc/status/2117429086448419000

What a backlog of this size means for people waiting

For the person whose case sits in the pile, the backlog is not an abstraction: it is the wait for a hearing at which asylum, family unity and the right to remain in the United States are decided. Cases are triaged, in the word used by Kansas City attorney Michael Sharma-Crawford, whose office described being forced to decide whom it can help and which immigrants will receive no help at all. The shortage is not only of judges. Genevra Alberti, immediate past chair of the Missouri/Kansas chapter of the American Immigration Lawyers Association, told The Pitch that the chapter has about 240 members, that less than half accept removal-defense cases, and that "there just are not enough attorneys to handle the volume." That matters because, unlike criminal court, immigration court carries no universal right to a government-appointed attorney — deportation is classified as a civil sanction. Only 23.4% of immigrants, including unaccompanied children, had an attorney with them when they were ordered removed in May 2025, according to government data compiled by TRAC and reported by The Pitch; the American Immigration Council has found that detained immigrants were more than 10 times as likely to successfully defend against deportation when represented by counsel.

"There just are not enough attorneys to handle the volume."

— Genevra Alberti, Missouri/Kansas AILA chapter, to The Pitch

What to do if your case is in this court

Three practical steps follow from how the system works. First, verify your hearing date rather than assuming a notice is current: EOIR's automated case information line is 800-898-7180, and the court's own page is maintained by the Department of Justice. Second, keep your mailing address updated with the court — hearing notices are mailed, and a missed hearing can result in a removal order issued in your absence. Third, seek counsel early: EOIR maintains a list of free and low-cost legal service providers for each court, and local organizations such as the Asylum Clinic Kansas City provide pro bono help for some categories of cases, including asylum cases of Afghans and unaccompanied children, according to The Pitch. Federal officials have responded to KMBC's reporting on the backlog and staffing, the station said; the structural question — how many judges and attorneys a two-state court needs — remains open.
